description: The War for Independence told through the national parks where it happened: Concord and Bunker Hill, Henry Knox's cannon train, Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell, Oriskany and Saratoga, Valley Forge, and the southern battles from Kings Mountain to Yorktown. Each day your child works through one free National Park Service lesson: maps, primary sources, a short reading, and a hands-on activity such as a reader's theater, a debate, or a STEM challenge. Every lesson plan and handout is free on nps.gov.
includes: 22 lessons in 5 units, from Lexington and Concord to Yorktown
Link to the National Park Service lesson page for every lesson, plus key handouts
Primary sources: orders, letters, maps, and the Articles of Capitulation
Reader's theater, debates, a STEM sled challenge, and a Valley Forge math lesson

units.title: Unit 1: 1775, the Shot Heard Round the World

lessons.title: Barrett Farm and the Start of the Revolution
steps: Read the background on Colonel James Barrett of Concord
Read the primary sources: the list of militia supplies, General Gage's orders, and Barrett's sworn statement
Use the evidence to write a short account of what Barrett did before and on April 19, 1775
Discuss: is every historical source equally reliable?

links.label: Lesson plan: Barrett Farm (Minute Man NHP)
Primary source 3: General Gage's orders (PDF)
Primary source 5: Barrett's deposition (PDF)

questions: Why did British troops march to Concord?
What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source?
answers: To find and destroy the colonists' military supplies, many kept under Colonel Barrett's care
A primary source was made by someone at the time; a secondary source was made later, about the event
lessons.notes: Written for high school; read the sources together and split them across two days for younger students.

lessons.title: The Battle of Bunker Hill: Now We Are at War
steps: Compare the Boston area today with the 1775 map
Read 'Setting the Stage for a Battle' and 'The Battle of Bunker Hill'
Activity: compare the colonists' rebellion with a protest or reform movement you know about

links.label: Lesson page: The Battle of Bunker Hill (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: On which hill was most of the 'Bunker Hill' fighting actually done?
What was the date of the battle?
The British won the hill. Why did the battle still encourage the colonists?
answers: Breed's Hill
The British lost so many men that the colonists saw they could stand up to the regular army

lessons.title: The Spark at Ticonderoga
steps: Find Fort Ticonderoga and Boston on a map of the northeastern colonies
Read the background on Henry Knox and his plan to haul the fort's cannons to Boston
Annotate the route map: mark rivers, mountains, and places where trouble could happen
Predict: will the plan work? List your reasons

links.label: Lesson plan: The Spark at Ticonderoga (Springfield Armory NHS)
Student map annotation activity (PDF)

questions: Why did the Continental Army near Boston need Knox's plan?
What job did Henry Knox have before the war?
Some of the cannons weighed over how many pounds?
answers: It had no heavy artillery to challenge the British in Boston
Bookseller in Boston
5,000 pounds

lessons.title: Ice, Iron, and the Hudson
steps: Study the Hudson corridor map and the photo of the frozen river
List ways to move heavy cannons in winter: sleds, skids, boats, roads; weigh pros and cons
STEM challenge: build a small sled from craft supplies and test how much weight it carries across a smooth 'frozen river'

links.label: Lesson plan: Ice, Iron, and the Hudson (Springfield Armory NHS)
Hudson corridor map (image)

questions: Why was the frozen Hudson both a help and a danger?
What problem-solving skills helped Knox's team succeed?
answers: Thick ice let sleds travel fast, but thin ice could break under the heavy guns
Adapting plans, teamwork, and creative thinking

lessons.title: The Turning Point in Springfield
steps: Read how Knox's train passed through Springfield, Massachusetts
Read the student-friendly version of Knox's 1777 letter to John Adams
Compare maps of Springfield and Boston and list what made Springfield a good supply depot
Write a short letter, as Knox, recommending Springfield

links.label: Lesson plan: The Turning Point in Springfield (Springfield Armory NHS)
Knox letter and student-friendly version (Word)

questions: Which river made Springfield useful for moving supplies?
To whom did Knox write in 1777 recommending Springfield over Brookfield?
answers: The Connecticut River
John Adams

units.title: Unit 2: 1776, Choosing Sides and Declaring Independence

lessons.title: Choosing Sides: Loyalist or Patriot?
steps: Read the two colonists' 'campaign speeches' aloud (one child or parent each)
Fill in the lesson's 'Which will you choose?' handout (on the lesson page): what would you gain or lose on each side?
Vote, then reveal which colonist was the Loyalist and which the Patriot

links.label: Lesson plan: Choosing Sides (Moores Creek NB)
Colonist A and B scripts (PDF)

questions: What is a Loyalist?
What is a Patriot?
answers: A colonist who stayed loyal to the British king
A colonist who supported independence from Britain

lessons.title: The Highland Scots at Moores Creek
steps: Look at the painting of the Battle of Moores Creek Bridge: what do you notice?
Read the lesson's short reading on Highland Scots who settled in North Carolina
Make a push and pull chart for why they came, then compare their experience with immigrants today

links.label: Lesson plan: The Highland Scots (Moores Creek NB)
Push and pull factor worksheet (PDF)

questions: Which side did many Highland Scots join at Moores Creek Bridge?
What are push and pull factors?
What had been removed from the bridge in the painting?
answers: The Loyalists
Reasons that push people to leave a place and pull them to a new one
The planks

lessons.title: Loyal to Whom?
steps: Answer: what does loyalty mean to you?
Watch the park's video clips about three neighbors near Saratoga: John Neilson, Jotham Bemus, and John Freeman
Sort their choices into Royalist, neutral, or supporter of independence, and list pros and cons of each

links.label: Lesson plan: Loyal to Whom? (Saratoga NHP)
Student activity packet (Word)

questions: Name the three main responses colonists had to independence.
Why might a family try to stay neutral?
answers: Royalist (Loyalist), neutral, or supporter of independence
They had friends or family on both sides, or a business that depended on both

lessons.title: Independence Hall: International Symbol of Freedom
steps: Find Philadelphia on the map of the thirteen colonies and the 1777 city plan
Read 'American Democracy Takes Shape' and the partial transcript of the Declaration of Independence
Read about the Constitution and about how the State House became a World Heritage Site
Activity: pick one signer and write a short profile

links.label: Lesson page: Independence Hall (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: What was Independence Hall called in 1776?
Which two founding documents were signed there?
In what year did it become a World Heritage Site?
answers: The Pennsylvania State House
The Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution

lessons.title: The Liberty Bell: From Obscurity to Icon
steps: Locate the Liberty Bell on the Philadelphia maps
Read 'The Growth of a Symbol' and 'The Crack in the Liberty Bell'
Read about the bell's tours and follow one trip on a map
Activity: design a symbol for something you believe in

links.label: Lesson page: The Liberty Bell (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: Who first called it the 'Liberty Bell'?
What year is cast on the bell?
answers: Abolitionist publications in the 1830s

lessons.title: The Battle of Oriskany: Blood Shed a Stream Running Down
steps: Trace the Great Carry trade route and the lands of the Iroquois Confederacy on the maps
Read 'Growing Tensions in Central New York' and 'The Battle of Oriskany'
Read about the battle's effects on neighbors and on the Haudenosaunee nations
Activity: 'Where Do I Stand?' Decide which side you would have chosen in the Mohawk Valley

links.label: Lesson page: The Battle of Oriskany (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: When was the Battle of Oriskany fought?
Which Iroquois nation's lands held the Great Carry trade route?
Why was Oriskany called a battle of neighbors?
answers: August 6, 1777
The Oneida Nation
Neighbors in the Mohawk Valley, both settlers and Native nations, fought on opposite sides

lessons.title: Saratoga: The Tide Turns on the Frontier
steps: Study the map of the Lake Champlain and Hudson Valley campaign
Read 'The Battles of Saratoga' and 'Eighteenth-Century Warfare'
Look at the French engraving of Burgoyne's surrender
Activity: hold a council of war as Burgoyne's officers: retreat, fight, or surrender?

links.label: Lesson: Saratoga, The Tide Turns on the Frontier (Teaching with Historic Places)

questions: Which British general surrendered at Saratoga?
Why is Saratoga called the turning point of the Revolution?
answers: John Burgoyne
The American victory encouraged France to join the war as an ally

lessons.title: Tradesmen of the Springfield Arsenal
steps: Read the arsenal's 'want ad' aloud
Take a tradesman role card (blacksmith, carpenter, wheelwright, and more) and read the bio sheet
Hold a 'town hall': explain why your trade matters to the army

links.label: Lesson plan: Tradesmen of the Springfield Arsenal (Springfield Armory NHS)
Tradesmen cards (Word)

questions: In what year was the Springfield Arsenal established?
What does a blacksmith do?
answers: Shapes iron into tools and parts, including parts for weapons

units.title: Unit 4: Valley Forge and the Soldiers Who Endured

lessons.title: The March In: Why Valley Forge?
steps: Brainstorm what you would look for in a winter campsite
Read the secondary sources and use the maps in 'The March In' handout
List the reasons Washington chose Valley Forge and score your group on the survival rubric

links.label: Lesson plan: The March In (Valley Forge NHP)
The March In: texts and maps (PDF)

questions: About how far was Valley Forge from British-held Philadelphia?
Name one reason the site was good for defense.
answers: About 20 miles
The high ground of Mount Joy and Mount Misery, with the Schuylkill River to the north

lessons.title: Valley Forge by the Numbers
steps: Watch the park film or read the talking points about the 1777 to 1778 encampment
Work the worksheet problems: food, firewood, and supplies for 12,000 soldiers
Discuss how the army's needs affected local farm families

links.label: Lesson plan: Valley Forge by the Numbers (Valley Forge NHP)

questions: Was Valley Forge a battle?
About how many men died of disease at Valley Forge?
Who trained the troops there?
answers: No, it was a winter encampment
About 1,700 to 2,000
Baron von Steuben

lessons.title: African Americans in the American Revolution
steps: Read the lesson's reading on African Americans in the Revolution
Choose one person from the reading and plan a mock interview
Design a stamp honoring that person and explain your choice

links.label: Lesson plan: African Americans in the American Revolution (Kings Mountain NMP)
Reading (PDF)

questions: About how many African Americans served in the war?
Why did many enslaved people join the British side?
answers: About 5,000
British commanders offered freedom to enslaved people who fought for the king

units.title: Unit 5: The Southern Campaign and Victory

lessons.title: Tactics in the Battle of Kings Mountain
steps: Read the lesson's reading on the battle and its terrain
Fill in a Venn diagram comparing Patriot and Loyalist tactics
Write a short advice column giving tactical tips to a soldier

links.label: Lesson plan: Tactics in the Battle of Kings Mountain (Kings Mountain NMP)
Reading: Tactics at Kings Mountain (PDF)

questions: What made Kings Mountain unusual among Revolutionary War battles?
Rifle or musket: which was more accurate, and which was faster to load?
answers: It was fought between Americans: no British troops served there
The rifle was more accurate; the musket was faster to load

lessons.title: Leaders at Cowpens: Morgan and Tarleton
steps: Read the background on Daniel Morgan and Banastre Tarleton
Make a two-column chart of each man's background and leadership style
Write a paragraph: how did leadership decide the battle?

links.label: Lesson plan: Leaders at the Battle of Cowpens (Cowpens NB)

questions: What job did Morgan have in the French and Indian War?
How did Morgan arrange his soldiers at Cowpens?
Why were Tarleton's men worn out when the battle began?
answers: Wagon driver (the 'Old Wagoner')
In three lines, so the militia could fire and fall back
He marched them from two in the morning with little food or rest

lessons.title: The Battle of Cowpens: Reader's Theater
steps: Read the teacher background on the people in the script
Perform the Cowpens reader's theater script together
Put the battle's events in order on the series-of-events chain

links.label: Lesson plan: Battle of Cowpens Reader's Theater (Cowpens NB)
Reader's theater script (Word)

questions: What was 'Tarleton's Quarter'?
On what date was the Battle of Cowpens fought?

January 17, 1781

lessons.title: Unsung Patriots: Women at Cowpens

links.label: Lesson plan: Unsung Patriots, Women at the Battle of Cowpens (Cowpens NB)

questions: What were 'camp followers'?

lessons.title: Guilford Courthouse: A Pivotal Battle

links.label: Lesson page: Guilford Courthouse (Teaching with Historic Places)
Full lesson plan (PDF)

questions: When was the battle fought?

To defeat at Yorktown, Virginia

lessons.title: Yorktown Through Poetry
